question: ⛔ Who is the operational owner for the enterprise network (name, role, on-call model) and who approves emergency changes?
rationale: Lack of clear ownership and escalation path leads to outages dragging on and unsafe changes during incidents.
evidence: RACI / support model document, CAB charter, discussion with NOC lead / IT operations manager.
red_flag: We kind of share it in the team or There is no formal CAB or emergency change process.

question: What is your official change-management process (normal vs emergency), and what are the standard lead times and blackout windows?
rationale: Misaligned lead times and blackout rules can derail migration waves or force risky after-hours changes.
evidence: Change-management policy, ITSM tool workflow (ServiceNow/Remedy), CAB minutes, discussion with change manager.
red_flag: We just send an email or There is no formal approval, we change whenever needed.

question: How is the NOC staffed (hours, on-site vs remote, L1/L2 split) and what tools do they use for monitoring and ticketing?
rationale: Understaffed or tool-poor NOC cannot detect or triage issues during and after cutover.
evidence: NOC runbook, tool inventory (SolarWinds, SevOne, ThousandEyes, etc.), discussion with NOC lead.
red_flag: Business hours only for a 24x7 business or We watch email instead of a real NMS.

question: What are your MTTR and SLA targets for critical network incidents, and are they currently being met?
rationale: Aggressive SLAs may require additional resiliency or rollback planning; chronic SLA breaches indicate underlying design or operations issues.
evidence: SLA documents, KPI dashboards, incident reports from ITSM, discussion with service owner.
red_flag: We do not track MTTR or SLA or We rarely meet our SLAs but nothing has been done.

question: Where are configuration backups stored, how frequently are they taken, and when was the last successful restore test per platform?
rationale: Lack of tested backups makes any failure or failed change potentially catastrophic.
evidence: NMS/backup tool (Cisco Catalyst Center, DNAC, Oxidized, RANCID, SolarWinds NCM), backup schedule, last restore test report.
red_flag: Backups run nightly but we never tested a restore or Some devices are not backed up.

question: Which devices are managed over the OOB network vs in-band, and how is OOB reachability monitored?
rationale: No or poorly monitored OOB makes recovery from control-plane or data-plane failures difficult during migration.
evidence: Network diagrams, IPAM entries for OOB ranges, console server inventory, monitoring tool config.
red_flag: We mostly SSH over the production network or We do not have dedicated OOB at key sites.

question: What is your standard for device software versions (golden images) and how do you track and enforce version compliance?
rationale: Mixed or unsupported code trains introduce unpredictable behavior and complicate TAC support and migration planning.
evidence: Software standards document, SWIM / Catalyst Center compliance reports, show version, show install summary.
red_flag: We upgrade when something breaks or Every device is on a different version.

question: How are syslog messages centralized and retained (servers, retention period, severity filters, secure transport)?
rationale: Poor logging or short retention hampers root-cause analysis and detecting subtle issues.
evidence: Syslog server configuration, show logging, SIEM dashboards, logging policy document.
red_flag: Only local logging or Syslog is sent but we never look at it / retention is a few days.

question: Which SNMP versions and communities/users are in use, and which NMS systems are authorized to poll or receive traps?
rationale: Weak SNMP security or undocumented NMS tools introduce security risk and noise.
evidence: show running-config | include snmp, NMS inventory, security standards.
red_flag: Public/private everywhere or We do not know all the systems polling the devices.

question: How is NTP provided and secured for network devices, and what is the expected max time skew across the estate?
rationale: Inconsistent time breaks log correlation, certificate-based VPN/auth, and troubleshooting timelines.
evidence: show ntp status, show ntp associations, NTP design document.
red_flag: We just point everything to some Internet server or Some devices do not run NTP.

question: What AAA architecture do you use for device logins (TACACS+/RADIUS), and what is the fallback behavior if AAA servers are unreachable?
rationale: Misconfigured AAA can lock out admins during cutover or allow uncontrolled local access if servers fail.
evidence: show running-config | section aaa, test aaa group, AAA runbook, security policy.
red_flag: If TACACS is down nobody can log in or Everyone shares a local admin account with no logging.

question: What is your standard maintenance window pattern (days, times, freeze periods) for network changes in production and DC?
rationale: Misaligned windows make realistic migration waves and rollback planning impossible.
evidence: Change calendar, CAB documentation, PMO schedule, discussion with change manager.
red_flag: We handle it ad-hoc or There are no defined maintenance windows for critical systems.

question: Which monitoring thresholds and alert rules currently generate the most noise, and how often are they tuned?
rationale: Noisy or untuned alerts cause alert fatigue and missed real issues during migration.
evidence: NMS alert configuration, monthly NOC reports, SIEM correlation rules.
red_flag: We ignore most alerts or Thresholds are default and never reviewed.

question: Who owns the standard network device hardening baseline, and how is compliance with it measured and enforced?
rationale: Lack of hardening exposes security risk and inconsistency (e.g., mgmt ACLs, SSH only, banner, password policy).
evidence: Hardening guideline, compliance reports from Catalyst Center or security tools, show running-config samples.
red_flag: There is no baseline or We have a document but nobody checks compliance.

question: How are ops handovers done after projects (runbooks, KB articles, training), and when was the last formal handover for the network?
rationale: Poor handover leaves NOC unable to support the new design, increasing MTTR and causing blame loops.
evidence: Previous project closure docs, runbooks, training schedules, discussion with PM and NOC lead.
red_flag: We just send configs or There is no formal handover, NOC figures it out.

question: What is the documented procedure to rapidly disable or roll back a faulty change during a live incident?
rationale: Lack of a tested rollback process turns small mistakes into major outages.
evidence: Change templates, emergency change SOP, incident postmortems.
red_flag: We just revert configs manually or It depends on who is on shift.

question: Which operational KPIs are regularly reported to management (availability, incident volume, change success rate), and how are they calculated?
rationale: Missing or misleading KPIs hide systemic issues and make it hard to show value of improvements.
evidence: KPI dashboards, monthly operations reports, IT governance documents.
red_flag: We do not have regular KPI reporting or The numbers are guessed, not automated.

question: ⛔ Have you tested a complete DR or site-failover scenario in the last 12–18 months, and what were the outcomes?
rationale: Untested DR failover can create surprises during real incidents or planned migrations.
evidence: DR test reports, DR runbooks, discussion with DR coordinator.
red_flag: Never tested or Last test failed and was not remediated.

question: Which parts of the network are considered safety-critical or life-safety (e.g., hospitals, industrial control), and what additional operational controls apply?
rationale: Safety-critical networks may require stricter change controls, redundancy, and rollback paths.
evidence: Safety impact assessment, facilities / OT documentation, discussion with safety officer or facilities manager.
red_flag: We are not sure or They are treated like normal office networks.

question: For third-party managed links or devices, what are the exact demarcation points, SLAs, and escalation paths during an outage?
rationale: Ambiguity about ownership at demarcation points causes long outages and finger-pointing.
evidence: Carrier contracts, managed service SOWs, escalation matrices.
red_flag: We open a generic ticket and wait or We do not have clear demarcation diagrams.

question: ⛔ What is the current high-level network topology (campus, WAN, DC, edge) and which design model are you targeting (three-tier, collapsed core, spine-leaf)?
rationale: Misaligned design intent leads to piecemeal changes that do not fit an overall architecture.
evidence: Latest HLD/LLD diagrams, enterprise architecture standards, discussions with network architect.
red_flag: We do not have up-to-date diagrams or It just grew organically.

question: Where are the Layer 2 and Layer 3 boundaries in the campus and DC today, and are there any stretched VLANs across sites?
rationale: Long L2 domains and stretched VLANs increase blast radius and STP complexity.
evidence: L2/L3 diagrams, show vlan, show spanning-tree, show ip interface brief.
red_flag: Many VLANs span multiple buildings/sites without clear justification.

question: Which modules of the Cisco enterprise architecture do you explicitly implement (campus, edge, branch, DC, teleworker) and which are missing or blurred?
rationale: Poor modularity complicates scaling, policy enforcement, and troubleshooting.
evidence: Enterprise architecture blueprint, design standards, discussion with enterprise architect.
red_flag: We do not follow any specific modular design or Everything is flat.

question: How are routing domains segmented (per site, per region, per function) and where are summarization points defined?
rationale: Lack of summarization causes large routing tables and slow convergence.
evidence: Routing design doc, show ip route, show ip ospf database, show bgp summary.
red_flag: We advertise everything everywhere with no summarization.

question: Which VLANs carry user access, voice, management, server, storage, and special-purpose traffic, and what is their IP addressing scheme?
rationale: Overloaded or unclear VLAN roles create security and broadcast-domain risks.
evidence: IP plan, show vlan brief, show ip interface brief, IPAM system.
red_flag: We reuse VLANs for multiple purposes or There is no central IP plan.

question: How is redundancy implemented at each layer (dual-homed access, distribution pairs, dual-homed WAN) and which failure scenarios have been explicitly tested?
rationale: Untested redundancy often fails under real failures, causing surprise outages.
evidence: HLD, test reports, show etherchannel summary, show standby, show vpc, show port-channel summary.
red_flag: We assume it works, but have never tested link/device failures systematically.

question: Where are the FHRP gateways located for user/server VLANs, and how are priorities, preemption, and tracking configured?
rationale: Misplaced gateways or misconfigured FHRP leads to asymmetric routing and longer failovers.
evidence: show standby brief, show glbp brief, show vrrp, L3 interface configs.
red_flag: Defaults everywhere with no tracking or Gateways unevenly spread with random priorities.

question: What is the target L3 design for access switches (L2-only, routed access, or a mix), and how does that align with your growth and segmentation needs?
rationale: A mix of L2/L3 access complicates policy, routing, and operations.
evidence: Campus design document, interface configs, show ip interface brief, show running-config interface.
red_flag: Some access switches are L3, some L2, for no documented reason.

question: How do you handle inter-VLAN routing and segmentation in the campus (SVIs on distribution, core, or firewall), and what is the long-term strategy?
rationale: Inconsistent default gateway placement complicates ACLs, QoS, and troubleshooting.
evidence: SVI configs, VRF definitions, firewall routing policy, L3 topology diagrams.
red_flag: Multiple devices provide inter-VLAN routing without a clear pattern.

question: Which routing protocols are used where (OSPF/EIGRP/BGP/ISIS/Static), and do you have a documented preference and design guide for each?
rationale: Mixed and ad-hoc protocol use creates complex redistribution and failure modes.
evidence: Routing design standard, show ip protocols, show ip ospf, show ip eigrp, show bgp summary.
red_flag: We use whatever the engineer preferred at the time without documentation.

question: How are failure domains constrained (e.g., access block, pair of distribution, spine-leaf pod), and what is the maximum acceptable blast radius?
rationale: Unbounded failure domains cause campus-wide or DC-wide impact from single failures.
evidence: Modular block diagrams, risk assessment doc, outage reports.
red_flag: A failure at distribution or aggregation typically affects the whole site.

question: What are your growth assumptions for users, branches, and DC capacity over the next 3–5 years, and how are address space and hardware sized for that?
rationale: Underestimating growth leads to renumbering, hardware replacement, or massive rework.
evidence: Capacity planning documents, IP addressing plan, hardware lifecycle roadmap.
red_flag: We do not have growth projections or We are almost out of VLANs/IPv4 space.

question: How is QoS implemented end-to-end (trust boundaries, markings, queuing policies), especially for voice, video, and critical apps?
rationale: Inconsistent QoS leads to poor performance under congestion despite bandwidth being sufficient.
evidence: QoS design doc, show policy-map interface, show mls qos, WAN provider QoS profile.
red_flag: QoS is configured only on some devices or We trust all markings from endpoints.

question: What are the current scalability constraints (TCAM limits, MAC table, ARP/ND, routing table size) on your key platforms?
rationale: Ignoring hardware limits can cause sudden control-plane failures as the network grows.
evidence: show platform hardware capacity or equivalent, CVDs and platform data sheets, SNMP stats.
red_flag: We have never checked platform limits or already high utilization with growth planned.

question: How do you enforce security zones and segmentation at the network layer (VRFs, firewalls, SGT/TrustSec, VRF-lite, SD-Access)?
rationale: Weak or inconsistent segmentation increases attack surface and complicates audits.
evidence: Security architecture docs, VRF config, firewall policy, ISE/SGT deployment plan.
red_flag: Mostly by VLAN only or Segmentation is ad-hoc via scattered ACLs.

question: How are Internet edges designed (single vs dual ISP, active/active vs active/standby, BGP policies), and what are the failure scenarios?
rationale: Poor Internet edge design causes outages or asymmetric routing during ISP issues.
evidence: Edge HLD, show bgp summary, show ip bgp, ISP contracts.
red_flag: Single ISP, single router for a critical business with no DR plan.

question: How is the DC fabric integrated with the campus and WAN (L3 handoff, VRFs, route leaking), and where are policy and inspection points placed?
rationale: Poor integration can create black holes, asymmetric flows, and security gaps between DC and users.
evidence: DC fabric design, border leaf configs, firewall topology diagrams.
red_flag: We just run a big OSPF area everywhere with firewalls inline randomly.

question: ⛔ Are there any undocumented or “special case” designs (hard-coded static routes, single-homed critical systems, bypass links) that operations relies on?
rationale: Hidden exceptions often break during cleanups or topology changes, causing surprise outages.
evidence: Interviews with senior engineers, static route configs, ad-hoc wiring diagrams.
red_flag: Yes, many, and they are only known by certain engineers with no documentation.

question: Which parts of the design explicitly follow Cisco Validated Designs or SAFE blueprints, and where have you knowingly deviated?
rationale: Deviations from known-good patterns may introduce unexpected behavior or unsupported topologies.
evidence: Design standards, CVD references, architecture review minutes.
red_flag: We are not aware of CVD/SAFE or We customized everything without rationale.

question: How is management traffic (SSH, SNMP, syslog, NetFlow, API) logically and physically separated from user and data traffic?
rationale: Mixing management and data planes increases security risk and makes DDoS more damaging.
evidence: Mgmt VRF/VLAN configs, out-of-band design, ACLs, show ip vrf, show run | sec line vty.
red_flag: All traffic including management goes over the same VLAN/VRF with no restrictions.

question: ⛔ Which exact sites, closets, or services are in scope for this migration phase, and which are explicitly out of scope?
rationale: Unclear scope leads to scope creep, missed dependencies, and cutover overruns.
evidence: Project charter, migration scope document, site list, inventory export from NMS.
red_flag: We will see during the cutover or Everything is in scope eventually, not sure for this wave.

question: What is the prioritized move-group strategy (by building, floor, closet, app, or user group), and how many endpoints are in each group?
rationale: Poorly defined move groups create oversized blasts and make rollback and troubleshooting hard.
evidence: Migration plan, endpoint inventory, CMDB, port usage reports, show mac address-table count.
red_flag: We are doing a big-bang at the whole campus in one night.

question: Which candidate sites/closets/users are selected for the pilot, and what makes them representative yet low-risk?
rationale: A non-representative pilot hides issues that will appear at scale; a high-risk pilot can damage confidence.
evidence: Pilot selection document, stakeholder interviews, historical incident data.
red_flag: Pilot is just IT department or Pilot is the most critical site with no rollback option.

question: What are the exact success criteria for the pilot (technical and business), and who signs off that they are met?
rationale: Without clear success criteria, the pilot cannot objectively gate the broader rollout.
evidence: Pilot test plan, UAT scripts, sign-off template, business owner interview.
red_flag: If there are no major complaints we move on with no documented tests.

question: Which hardware and software compatibility checks have been done (feature support, license levels, memory/TCAM/scale) for the target platforms?
rationale: Missing compatibility checks lead to in-window surprises like unsupported features or scale exhaustion.
evidence: BOM, release notes, Cisco Feature Navigator output, show version, show platform hardware capacity.
red_flag: We ordered similar hardware but did not check code or feature support in detail.

question: How are old-to-new port mappings and VLAN/VRF mappings defined and validated per device and per closet?
rationale: Incorrect mappings cause wrong endpoint placement, outages, and lengthy rework during cutover.
evidence: Detailed MoP, port-mapping spreadsheets, show cdp neighbor, show lldp neighbor, rack diagrams.
red_flag: We will map cables on the fly or Only high-level mapping, no per-port view.

question: What lab or staging validation has been done with the new configs (routing adjacencies, FHRP behavior, 802.1X, DHCP relay, QoS)?
rationale: Lack of pre-validation pushes basic config errors into the production window.
evidence: Lab test report, staging logs, show ip ospf neighbor, show standby, RADIUS logs, DHCP logs.
red_flag: No lab; we will test in production or Only ping tested, no protocol or auth validation.

question: How will you freeze non-essential changes on the legacy network during the migration (who enforces the change freeze and for how long)?
rationale: Concurrent unrelated changes can mask issues and break assumptions used in migration planning.
evidence: Change freeze announcement, CAB decisions, RFC list, change calendar.
red_flag: There is no freeze; changes will continue as usual.

question: What are the standard pre-checks for each cut (interfaces, routing, spanning tree, authentication, syslog/NTP/AAA reachability), and who runs them?
rationale: Missing pre-checks make it impossible to distinguish pre-existing issues from migration defects.
evidence: MoP checklist, show ip interface brief, show cdp neighbor, show spanning-tree, show logging, show ntp status, test aaa group.
red_flag: We will check basic pings only or no repeatable pre-check template.

question: What are the standard post-checks and validation tests (per VLAN, per SSID, per VRF, per critical app) and the exact pass/fail thresholds?
rationale: Incomplete post-checks may miss issues that only appear under specific flows or user groups.
evidence: MoP, UAT scripts, show ip route, show mac address-table, application smoke tests, synthetic transaction results.
red_flag: We just see if users complain or No formal list; the engineer decides.

question: ⛔ What is the step-by-step rollback plan for each change, including time to execute, dependencies, and who approves invoking it?
rationale: Without a tested rollback, GO/NO-GO decisions become emotional and outages may be prolonged.
evidence: MoP rollback section, config backup repository, test rollback report, CAB agreement.
red_flag: Rollback is copy-pasting the old config; we have not timed it or Rollback is not documented.

question: How will traffic be re-routed away from devices being migrated, and what are the interim routing or STP states you expect?
rationale: Unexpected transient states can create loops, black holes, or asymmetry during the cut.
evidence: Interim design diagrams, show ip route, show spanning-tree root, show etherchannel summary, MoP step sequence.
red_flag: We will shut down links and hope routing reconverges quickly with no modeling.

question: What is the communication plan to end users and stakeholders before, during, and after each cut window?
rationale: Poor communication leads to confusion, duplicate incidents, and perception of instability.
evidence: Project communication plan, email templates, service status portal entries.
red_flag: We will send one email at the start of the project or no defined comms.

question: Who has real-time authority during the cut window to decide GO/NO-GO, rollback, or extend the change window?
rationale: Ambiguity about decision-making can waste time and extend outages during issues.
evidence: RACI matrix, change record, escalation plan, presence list for cutover bridge.
red_flag: We will decide as a group with no named accountable owner.

question: What additional monitoring or telemetry will be enabled during migration (NetFlow, SPAN, synthetic transactions, extra syslog) and how will it be consumed?
rationale: Lack of enhanced observability makes it difficult to distinguish migration defects from normal noise.
evidence: NMS configuration, test harnesses, traffic generator configs.
red_flag: We will use existing monitoring only, no special views or dashboards.

question: How is resource coverage organized during the window (L1/L2/L3 network, security, app owners, voice, vendor TAC on standby)?
rationale: Missing key SMEs during a cut window turns solvable issues into long outages.
evidence: Cutover staffing plan, on-call schedule, TAC case pre-opened.
red_flag: Only one network engineer on site for a large or critical migration.

question: What is the acceptance period after each wave (stabilization window) before proceeding to the next wave?
rationale: Moving too quickly hides latent problems; moving too slowly can lose momentum and budget.
evidence: Migration plan, CAB approvals, KPI trends post-wave.
red_flag: We will cut everything in consecutive nights regardless of issues.

question: How will configuration drift between staged configs and production be detected and remediated during the program?
rationale: Drift erodes the value of standardized templates and complicates support.
evidence: Config management tool reports, Catalyst Center compliance, periodic show running-config audits.
red_flag: We sometimes tweak configs manually; there is no drift detection.

question: After decommission, how are old devices wiped, inventory updated, and support contracts adjusted?
rationale: Forgotten devices and contracts create security risk and unnecessary cost.
evidence: Asset management process, CMDB updates, RMA/return procedures, security standards.
red_flag: We just power them off and leave them in the rack.

question: ⛔ If a migration wave fails partially (some closets/sites OK, others not), what is the policy: partial rollback vs targeted rollback vs full rollback?
rationale: Lack of a nuanced policy forces all-or-nothing decisions that either overreact or underreact to issues.
evidence: Migration strategy document, CAB guidance, risk register.
red_flag: We will decide ad-hoc in the bridge with no guiding principle.

question: Which STP mode is running in the campus (PVST+/Rapid-PVST+/MST) and where are the root bridges for each VLAN or instance?
rationale: Unknown or inconsistent STP design leads to suboptimal paths and high risk of loops.
evidence: show spanning-tree summary, show spanning-tree root, campus design doc.
red_flag: Defaults everywhere or We do not control where STP roots are.

question: Are STP protections such as BPDU Guard, Root Guard, and Loop Guard enabled on appropriate ports, especially at the access edge?
rationale: Lack of STP protections makes the network vulnerable to user-induced loops or rogue switches.
evidence: show spanning-tree summary, show spanning-tree interface detail, interface configs.
red_flag: We do not use those features or Only on a few switches with no standard.

question: How are FHRPs (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP) deployed per VLAN, and which device is primary vs secondary in each failure domain?
rationale: Misaligned or asymmetric gateway placement causes suboptimal paths and unpredictable failovers.
evidence: show standby brief, show vrrp, show glbp brief, gateway design tables.
red_flag: We configured them once and never revisited priorities or tracking.

question: What tracking objects (interfaces, IP SLA, routes) are tied to FHRP priorities, and have failover scenarios been tested recently?
rationale: Missing or untested tracking causes FHRP to remain active even when key paths are down.
evidence: show standby, show track, show ip sla config, failover test reports.
red_flag: No tracking configured or We never test FHRP failovers.

question: How are EtherChannel/port-channel bundles formed (LACP/PAgP/on), and do you have any mismatches or single-link bundles?
rationale: Misconfigured port-channels cause one-way links or unexpected blocking states.
evidence: show etherchannel summary, show interface port-channel, logs for bundle flaps.
red_flag: We use mode on everywhere or frequent individual link flaps in bundles.

question: How are access ports classified (user, voice, AP, trunk, server) and what default switchport templates or macros are applied?
rationale: Inconsistent edge configurations lead to unpredictable behavior, QoS, and security exposure.
evidence: show running-config interface, switchport templates, Catalyst Center templates.
red_flag: Each engineer configures ports differently with no templates.

question: Which IGP is used in the campus (EIGRP/OSPF/ISIS) and which in the WAN, and how are they redistributed at boundaries?
rationale: Complex or uncontrolled redistribution causes routing loops, black holes, and slow convergence.
evidence: show ip protocols, show ip ospf, show ip eigrp topology, redistribution configs.
red_flag: We redistribute everything into everything with no filtering or tagging.

question: What OSPF area design do you use (backbone, regular, stub, NSSA), and where are ABRs and ASBRs located?
rationale: Poor OSPF area design leads to large LSDBs, slow convergence, and complex troubleshooting.
evidence: show ip ospf, show ip ospf database, OSPF design doc.
red_flag: Single area for entire network or Areas added randomly without plan.

question: In EIGRP environments, what are the autonomous system boundaries and summarization points, and is wide-metric (EIGRP named mode) used?
rationale: Lack of summarization and outdated metrics can cause convergence and scale issues.
evidence: show ip eigrp topology, show running-config | section router eigrp, platform CVDs.
red_flag: No summarization or Classic EIGRP everywhere with no plan to migrate.

question: How is BGP used (Internet edge, MPLS WAN, DC interconnect), and what is the policy for prefix filtering, communities, and path control?
rationale: Weak BGP policy can leak routes, cause suboptimal paths, or expose the network to DFZ issues.
evidence: show bgp summary, show ip bgp, route-maps, prefix-lists, ISP peering docs.
red_flag: We accept and advertise everything or no documentation of BGP policies.

question: Are VRFs used for segmentation (user vs management vs guest vs partner), and how many VRFs and routes per VRF are in use on key devices?
rationale: VRF sprawl or core devices at scale limits create TCAM pressure and complexity.
evidence: show vrf, show ip route vrf <name>, platform capacity reports.
red_flag: We keep adding VRFs for every new case without consolidation or review.

question: How is QoS implemented end-to-end (classification, marking, queuing, shaping) on both campus and WAN, and where are trust boundaries?
rationale: Misaligned QoS policies cause critical apps to suffer during congestion despite available tools.
evidence: QoS design doc, show policy-map interface, show mls qos, provider QoS profiles.
red_flag: QoS is only configured on WAN edge or We trust markings from all endpoints.

question: Which multicast routing protocol is used (PIM-SM/SSM/Bidir) and where are RP(s) defined and any MSDP or BSR roles?
rationale: Poor multicast design leads to flooding, black holes, or dependency on a single RP.
evidence: show ip pim neighbor, show ip pim rp, show ip mroute, multicast design docs.
red_flag: We enabled PIM by default or We do not know where the RP is.

question: How do you handle multicast in the WAN (native, GRE, mVPN, or head-end replication) and what scale limits have been considered?
rationale: Unsupported or unscaled multicast over WAN can break as sources or receivers grow.
evidence: WAN design documents, SP handoff details, show ip mroute, show interfaces accounting.
red_flag: We rely on provider magic or We tunnel everything without scale testing.

question: What fast convergence mechanisms are enabled (BFD, tuned hello/dead timers, LFA/FRR, NSF/SSO) and where?
rationale: Missing fast convergence can cause noticeable outages for voice, trading, or OT.
evidence: show bfd neighbors, show ip ospf interface, show ip route, platform HA configs.
red_flag: We use default timers or No BFD anywhere for low-latency apps.

question: Are any legacy protocols still in use (HSRPv1, RIPv2, EoL STP modes, static WRED configs) that might limit future migrations?
rationale: Legacy protocols hinder migration to modern designs and may be unsupported in new platforms.
evidence: show ip protocols, show standby, show spanning-tree, device EoL/EoS notices.
red_flag: Yes, many, but nobody wants to touch them.

question: How is IPv6 deployed (dual stack, tunnels, none), and what is the roadmap for IPv6-only or IPv6-preferred services?
rationale: Lack of IPv6 planning can hinder new services and cloud integration.
evidence: IPv6 design docs, show ipv6 interface, show ipv6 route.
red_flag: We ignore IPv6 or scattered, undocumented IPv6 usage.

question: How are management and telemetry flows (SSH, SNMP, syslog, NetFlow/sFlow) routed and secured (VRF, ACLs, firewalls)?
rationale: Poorly isolated management traffic increases exposure to attack and DDoS.
evidence: show ip vrf, management ACLs, firewall rules, SIEM integration docs.
red_flag: Same VRF as user traffic with no ACL restrictions.

question: Which WAN technologies are in use (MPLS, SD-WAN, Internet VPN, private fiber), and where is policy and path selection applied?
rationale: Overlapping technologies without clear policy cause asymmetric routing and troubleshooting issues.
evidence: WAN design docs, SD-WAN controller policies, show ip route, show sdwan omp peers (if applicable).
red_flag: Multiple overlapping solutions with no clear strategy.

question: Are any critical apps or services sensitive to latency, jitter, or loss (voice, video, trading, control systems), and how do you measure and enforce performance?
rationale: Ignoring app performance needs leads to outages that look fine at the network layer.
evidence: App inventory, QoS design docs, IP SLA/Telemetry, show ip sla statistics.
red_flag: We rely on best-effort or Users complain but we have no SLOs.

question: Which Nexus platforms and NX-OS versions are in use in each DC, and what is the standard code (golden image) target?
rationale: Mixed hardware and software without a standard complicate features like vPC, VXLAN, and in-service upgrades.
evidence: Asset inventory, show version, DC design standards.
red_flag: Every pair runs a different release or We upgrade only when something breaks.

question: How are vPC domains structured (which pairs, where, for what roles) and how is peer-link/keepalive connectivity designed and monitored?
rationale: Weak vPC design or monitoring can lead to vPC split-brain, orphaned ports, or unexpected outages.
evidence: show vpc, show vpc role, show int port-channel, topology diagrams.
red_flag: We have vPC but do not monitor peer-link or keepalive health.

question: Are any classic vPC-based DC designs being migrated to a VXLAN-EVPN fabric, and what is the coexistence/transition strategy?
rationale: Poor transition can lead to duplicate gateways, loops, or black holes at the vPC–VXLAN boundary.
evidence: Migration HLD, show vlan, show nve peers, show l2route evpn, DCI design docs.
red_flag: We will just connect the new fabric to the old core and see with no plan.

question: What is the underlay routing design for the DC fabric (IGP, addressing, loopbacks), and are all links point-to-point with consistent MTU?
rationale: Weak underlay leads to intermittent VXLAN issues that are hard to diagnose.
evidence: show ip ospf neighbor or show isis neighbor, show interface, underlay addressing plan.
red_flag: It uses a mix of static routes and OSPF with default configs.

question: How is the overlay implemented (VXLAN flood-and-learn vs VXLAN-EVPN), and which nodes act as VTEPs and border gateways?
rationale: Non-unified overlay strategy may break mobility and segmentation or complicate DCI.
evidence: show nve interface, show nve peers, show bgp l2vpn evpn, VXLAN design doc.
red_flag: Some devices run VXLAN, others rely on stretching VLANs, with no clear plan.

question: How are VNIs mapped to VLANs and VRFs, and is there a consistent numbering scheme across the fabric and sites?
rationale: Inconsistent mappings cause operational confusion, misrouting, and migration mistakes.
evidence: show nve vni, show vlan, show vrf, mapping spreadsheet.
red_flag: Mappings are ad-hoc per engineer or We reuse VNIs with different meanings.

question: What is the DCI strategy (EVPN Multi-site, OTV, vPC BGW, L3 DCI only), and which VLANs or VRFs require stretching vs L3 only?
rationale: Poor DCI design extends failure domains or breaks app dependencies during failover.
evidence: DCI design doc, show bgp l2vpn evpn, show vxlan evpn multicast, show nve multisite.
red_flag: We stretch almost all VLANs between DCs by default.

question: What oversubscription ratios exist at server access, aggregation, and uplinks, and are they acceptable for expected east-west and north-south patterns?
rationale: Excessive oversubscription causes congestion and latency at peak, especially during failure.
evidence: Port speed inventory, traffic graphs, show interface counters, DC capacity plan.
red_flag: We do not know or ratios like 20:1+ on critical tiers without justification.

question: How are server NICs connected (single-homed vs dual-homed, vPC, LACP, UCS FI uplinks), and what is the failover behavior?
rationale: Single-homed critical servers or badly configured LACP can cause outages on link or node failure.
evidence: show port-channel summary, NIC teaming policies, UCS FI configs, Nutanix cluster docs.
red_flag: Many critical servers are single-homed or Various untested teaming modes.

question: For UCS, what is the vNIC/vHBA policy model (templates, QoS policies) and how does it map to upstream network VLANs and VNIs?
rationale: Misaligned policies between UCS and network fabric can cause VLAN mis-tags and congestion.
evidence: UCS service profile templates, vNIC policy docs, show run vlan on upstream switches.
red_flag: Each blade has custom vNICs with no global templates or documentation.

question: For Nutanix or other HCI, how are storage, management, and VM networks separated (VLAN/VRF), and what MTU is used end-to-end?
rationale: Inconsistent MTU or mixing storage and user traffic can cause performance and stability issues.
evidence: Nutanix networking design, show interface, show system mtu, hypervisor vSwitch configs.
red_flag: All traffic uses one VLAN at 1500 MTU for simplicity for storage-intensive workloads.

question: How is storage traffic carried (NFS/iSCSI/FCoE/FC), and are dedicated networks/fabrics and QoS policies in place for it?
rationale: Storage performance and stability degrade if it competes with regular traffic on oversubscribed links.
evidence: Storage network design, SAN fabric diagrams, show interface, QoS configs.
red_flag: Storage shares the same VLAN and QoS as user traffic with no guarantees.

question: How are tenant or environment boundaries modeled (VRFs, separate fabrics, ACI tenants, firewalls), and what is the maximum number of tenants?
rationale: Poor multi-tenancy can lead to noisy-neighbor issues and complex routing.
evidence: VRF configuration, fabric tenant list, show vrf, security design docs.
red_flag: We just use VLANs for everything in a multi-tenant DC.

question: What is the DC-wide default gateway strategy (anycast gateway with IRB/SVI on VTEPs vs centralized gateways), and how was it tested?
rationale: Inconsistent gateway placement breaks mobility and can cause asymmetric routing.
evidence: show ip arp, show ip route vrf, show nve vni, fabric HLD.
red_flag: Some VLANs use local VTEP gateway, others centralized, with no documentation.

question: Are there any bare-metal or special workloads (e.g., appliances, clustered DB, media, GPUs) with nonstandard network requirements?
rationale: Special workloads may need jumbo frames, pinning, or strict latency that generic design misses.
evidence: App requirements docs, interviews with app owners, show interface, hypervisor configs.
red_flag: Yes, but nobody knows their exact requirements.

question: How is management of DC devices handled (OOB network, mgmt VRFs, jump hosts), and is it fully separated from tenant/data traffic?
rationale: Weak management isolation increases security risk and complicates during-incident access.
evidence: Mgmt network design, show ip vrf, show interface mgmt0, firewall policies.
red_flag: We manage devices over production VRFs shared with tenant traffic.

question: What is the patching and upgrade strategy for DC switches, UCS, hypervisors, and storage, and have you tested ISSU/maintenance-mode flows?
rationale: Poorly planned upgrades cause long outages, fabric splits, or cluster instability.
evidence: Maintenance plans, previous change records, show install all status, UCS/hypervisor patch schedules.
red_flag: Upgrades are ad-hoc and often skipped until mandatory.

question: How are telemetry and visibility implemented (DCNM/Nexus Dashboard, streaming telemetry, SPAN/ERSPAN, flow analytics)?
rationale: Lack of deep visibility in DC makes east-west issues very hard to troubleshoot.
evidence: Nexus Dashboard/DCNM configs, telemetry platform, show monitor, show system resources.
red_flag: Only basic SNMP and syslog in a complex fabric.

question: ⛔ What are the DC failover and DR scenarios (intra-DC, inter-DC, cloud) and how often are they tested end-to-end with real applications?
rationale: Unplanned DR behavior can cause prolonged outages during real events or planned site migrations.
evidence: DR runbooks, test reports, DCI design.
red_flag: Failover is theoretical; we have never done a full test.

question: What are the target oversubscription limits you are willing to accept per tier (server-access, aggregation, DCI), and who owns those decisions?
rationale: Without explicit limits, capacity decisions are arbitrary and can degrade over time.
evidence: Capacity planning documents, DC architecture governance.
red_flag: We do not define oversubscription; we add links when things feel slow.

question: Which critical applications and business services exist, and for each, who is the named application owner or SME?
rationale: Without clear app owners, you cannot validate behavior, schedule downtime, or triage issues during cutover.
evidence: CMDB/service catalog, app portfolio, interviews with app owners and business relationship managers.
red_flag: We do not have an app catalog or Ownership is unclear for many critical apps.

question: How are applications mapped to network constructs today (VLANs, VRFs, subnets, firewall zones, SGTs), and is there a maintained mapping document?
rationale: Missing mapping forces guesswork when segmenting, migrating, or troubleshooting.
evidence: Network segmentation matrix, firewall policy, ISE/TrustSec design, IPAM.
red_flag: We know roughly or No single source of truth for app-to-network mapping.

question: For each critical app, what are the typical source and destination subnets/ports/protocols, and are any nonstandard or dynamic ports used?
rationale: Unclear flows break during segmentation, firewall tightening, or path changes.
evidence: Firewall logs, NetFlow/sFlow data, application documentation, discussions with app teams.
red_flag: We open any-any or Nobody knows exact ports; we will see what breaks.

question: Which applications have strict latency/jitter/loss requirements, and what current performance do you observe under peak conditions?
rationale: Latency-sensitive apps need special QoS and topology consideration.
evidence: App performance SLOs, latency measurement tools, IP SLA, voice quality reports.
red_flag: We do not measure or Users complain but we have no metrics.

question: Are there any broadcast, multicast, or PTP-based services (IPTV, market data, industrial control, media clocks) and where do their senders/receivers reside?
rationale: Broadcast/multicast/PTP flows are sensitive to topology and can break with small changes.
evidence: Application design docs, show ip mroute, show pim neighbor, show ptp clock.
red_flag: Yes, but we don't know exact scope or They rely on flat L2 everywhere.

question: For voice and video, what call-control platforms and endpoints are in use, and how are they logically separated (VLAN/VRF, QoS markings)?
rationale: Voice/video need consistent QoS, VLANs, and possibly separate security zones.
evidence: Call control design docs, show vlan, QoS configs, phone config templates.
red_flag: Phones share data VLAN and no QoS or inconsistent DSCP markings.

question: What batch jobs or large data transfers (backups, ETL, replication) run on a schedule, and do they overlap with planned maintenance windows?
rationale: Heavy batch jobs can mask or exacerbate network issues during cutover.
evidence: Backup schedules, job schedulers, storage replication configs, NetFlow analysis.
red_flag: Backups run all night with no coordination with network changes.

question: For each app, what is the tolerance for outage or degraded performance (RTO/RPO, maintenance window length, maximum downtime)?
rationale: Mismatched expectations can make normal migration impact look like an incident.
evidence: Business continuity plans, app SLO documents, DR runbooks.
red_flag: We expect zero downtime without HA licensing or architecture.

question: How are dependencies between applications modeled (DBs, messaging buses, APIs, directory services), and is there a dependency map?
rationale: Hidden dependencies can break when IPs/subnets/zones change.
evidence: Dependency mapping tools, app architecture diagrams, interviews with architects.
red_flag: We discover dependencies only when things break.

question: Which applications rely on client IP for access control (e.g., IP whitelists in apps/databases) instead of identity-based controls?
rationale: IP-based policies must be updated during renumbering or VRF/VLAN changes, or they will silently block access.
evidence: Application firewall configs, DB ACLs, web server configs, app SME interviews.
red_flag: Many critical apps use hard-coded IP whitelists with no central list.

question: How are DNS names and records used by the apps (A, CNAME, SRV, PTR), and do any apps use hard-coded IPs or local hosts files?
rationale: Hard-coded IPs bypass DNS and fail after renumbering or topology change.
evidence: DNS zone files, app documentation, server configs, hosts file reviews.
red_flag: Several legacy apps hard-code IPs with no plan to fix.

question: For east-west traffic within DCs, what percentage of flows are intra-tier vs inter-tier vs cross-zone/site, and how is that measured?
rationale: Understanding east-west patterns is key to fabric design and segmentation strategy.
evidence: NetFlow/sFlow, telemetry dashboards, DC traffic analysis reports.
red_flag: We have no visibility; we only monitor north-south flows.

question: Are there any applications that use L2 adjacency or rely on ARP broadcasts or non-IP protocols across racks or sites?
rationale: L2 dependencies constrain how far you can push L3 boundaries and VXLAN/EVPN segmentation.
evidence: Packet captures, app documentation, show mac address-table, SME interviews.
red_flag: Some legacy apps require flat L2 across the DC with no migration plan.

question: For PTP or other timing-sensitive apps, how are timing domains, grandmasters, and boundary clocks designed across the network?
rationale: Poor PTP design can break broadcast/media timing, trading timestamps, or industrial control.
evidence: show ptp clock, show ptp port, PTP design documentation.
red_flag: We just plugged in PTP sources without a formal timing design.

question: How are authentication and authorization integrated into applications (Kerberos/LDAP/SAML/OAuth), and do network changes affect these flows?
rationale: Directory/auth flows often cross zones and can be broken by firewall changes or DNS/IP shifts.
evidence: Identity architecture diagrams, IdP configs, firewall rules, app configs.
red_flag: We are not sure where auth flows traverse in a highly segmented environment.

question: What are the monitoring and APM tools for applications (APM, synthetics, RUM), and do they expose per-transaction latency and errors?
rationale: Without app-level metrics, network changes may get blamed for unrelated app issues.
evidence: Tools like AppDynamics, Dynatrace, New Relic, synthetic monitoring configs.
red_flag: We only know an app is down when users call the helpdesk.

question: Which apps are multi-region or multi-DC active-active, and how is traffic steered (GSLB/DNS, anycast, BGP)?
rationale: Active-active apps have special requirements for routing, health checks, and data consistency.
evidence: GSLB configs, DNS policies, BGP design, app HA docs.
red_flag: We advertise the same VIP from two DCs without clear data sync strategy.

question: Are there regulatory or compliance-driven requirements for specific apps (PCI, HIPAA, data residency) that impact network design or telemetry?
rationale: Ignoring compliance can lead to audit failures and expensive retrofits.
evidence: Compliance documentation, security policies, auditor reports.
red_flag: We are not sure which apps are in scope for which regulations.

question: During prior network changes, which specific applications caused the most issues or surprise outages, and why?
rationale: Historical problem apps highlight hidden dependencies or fragile protocols.
evidence: Incident postmortems, change records, interviews with NOC and app owners.
red_flag: We do not perform postmortems or recurring app names with no remediation.

question: ⛔ For each critical app, who will be on the bridge during cutovers, and what specific tests will they run to confirm functionality?
rationale: Without engaged app owners and clear tests, GO/NO-GO decisions become guesswork.
evidence: Cutover staffing plan, UAT scripts, sign-off checklist.
red_flag: App teams are not required to attend or No defined tests; we will rely on pings.

question: Which firewall platforms and software versions are in use (ASA, FTD, others), and what is the standard/golden version target?
rationale: Mixed or outdated code can introduce bugs, missing features, and security vulnerabilities that affect migration safety.
evidence: Asset inventory, show version (ASA/FTD), FMC device summary, security standards.
red_flag: Each firewall runs a different release or We only upgrade when TAC tells us.

question: How are firewalls deployed logically (routed, transparent, one-arm, virtual contexts/tenants), and where are the trust boundaries/zones defined?
rationale: Unclear deployment modes and zones lead to inconsistent policy and unexpected bypass paths.
evidence: Network/security HLD, show run | i interface|nameif (ASA), FMC policy and zone view.
red_flag: We use a mix of modes with no documentation of why or Zones are not clearly defined.

question: What is the current security policy model (inside-to-outside default allow vs default deny) and how strictly is egress filtering enforced?
rationale: Overly permissive policies increase attack surface and make segmentation projects harder.
evidence: ASA/FTD ACLs, FMC access policy, security policy documents.
red_flag: Inside is allowed to go anywhere by default with no explicit egress rules.

question: How are NAT policies structured (object NAT, manual NAT, twice NAT), and is there a clear separation between internal, DMZ, and external NAT rules?
rationale: Messy NAT order and rules cause hard-to-debug connectivity and migration issues.
evidence: show nat detail (ASA/FTD), FMC NAT policy view, NAT design doc.
red_flag: NAT grew organically or We do not fully understand NAT order-of-operation.

question: Which rules are actually hit frequently vs rarely (top-talkers, shadowed rules, expired objects), and how often is rule hygiene reviewed?
rationale: Stale or shadowed rules hide real dependencies and bloat policy, increasing risk and migration effort.
evidence: FMC hit count reports, ASA show access-list counters, rule review reports.
red_flag: We never remove rules or Hit counters are not reviewed.

question: Are there any any-any or wide-open rules in production, and what business justification and time-bound exceptions exist for them?
rationale: Wide-open rules are high-risk and must be remediated or handled carefully in migrations.
evidence: ACL entries, FMC policy search, exception approval records.
red_flag: Several any-any rules exist because we had issues before with no end date.

question: How are failover and clustering implemented (HA pairs, multi-context, FMC HA), and have you done a controlled failover test recently?
rationale: Unverified HA leads to outages when a real failure or maintenance event occurs.
evidence: show failover (ASA), show cluster info, FMC HA state, failover test reports.
red_flag: We rely on HA but never test failovers or Standby units are out of sync.

question: How is traffic inspection configured for key protocols (HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, SIP, FTP, etc.), and have you disabled any default inspections due to issues?
rationale: Inspection anomalies can break applications during or after migration, especially with new flows or NAT.
evidence: Policy-map/class-map configs, FMC access/security policies, show service-policy.
red_flag: We disable many inspections blindly when apps break or no record of which were changed.

question: What is the behavior on failure for inline features (IPS, AMP, URL filtering)—fail-open or fail-closed—and is that acceptable for each traffic class?
rationale: Wrong fail-open/closed posture can either cause outages or silently bypass security during failures.
evidence: FMC security policy, ASA service-policy configs, security policy standards.
red_flag: Defaults only, nobody reviewed fail-open vs fail-closed per link.

question: How are management and logging handled (syslog destinations, levels, timestamps, CEF export), and who monitors firewall events?
rationale: Poor logging and monitoring hide ongoing attacks and make troubleshooting very difficult.
evidence: Syslog server configs, show logging, FMC logging policy, SIEM integration.
red_flag: We log to local buffer only or Nobody actively reviews firewall logs.

question: How is inter-zone segmentation implemented (L3 zones, VRFs, SGTs, separate contexts), and do you follow a documented zoning model (e.g., PCI, OT)?
rationale: Ad-hoc segmentation creates inconsistent access and audit/compliance issues.
evidence: Security zoning document, firewall context/VRF design, ISE/SGT policy.
red_flag: Zones are created on demand per project with no global framework.

question: Are there specific app or vendor requirements that forced policy exceptions (e.g., pinholes, static NAT to internal admin interfaces), and are they documented?
rationale: Hidden exceptions often break during cleanup or platform migration, causing outages.
evidence: Exception register, ticket history, app owner interviews, firewall configs.
red_flag: Yes, but they are only known by one or two engineers.

question: How are SSL/TLS inspections or offload handled (if at all), and have you accounted for certificate pinning or privacy constraints?
rationale: Misconfigured TLS inspection breaks modern apps and can violate compliance rules.
evidence: SSL inspection policy, CA hierarchy docs, app testing reports.
red_flag: We do not know which apps break with SSL inspection, so we keep adding bypasses.

question: For remote management access, what controls are in place (management-only ACLs, jump hosts, MFA), and are they separate from data-plane rules?
rationale: Weak management access controls expose the firewall itself to compromise.
evidence: Management ACLs, show running-config | include ssh|http, PAM/jump host design.
red_flag: We permit SSH/ASDM from any for convenience.

question: ⛔ During migration, will any traffic paths bypass the firewall (e.g., temporary L2 links, side routers), and if so, how is that risk mitigated?
rationale: Temporary bypass paths create security blind spots and possible policy violations.
evidence: Migration HLD, interim topology diagrams, MoP, security review sign-offs.
red_flag: Yes, some traffic will bypass temporarily, but we have no compensating controls.

question: How do you manage policy changes (ticketing, peer review, change windows), and are rule changes auditable per request?
rationale: Uncontrolled policy changes create drift and make troubleshooting and compliance harder.
evidence: Change tickets, firewall change logs, FMC/ASA config history, security operations SOP.
red_flag: Engineers change rules directly on the device without tickets.

question: How are VPN termination and firewall roles split (same boxes vs separate), and can VPN changes impact firewall throughput or vice versa?
rationale: Overloading a firewall with VPN and firewalling can cause performance issues after growth or migrations.
evidence: Topology diagrams, show crypto ipsec sa, show asp drop, performance baselines.
red_flag: All VPN and firewall functions are on a single undersized pair.

question: Are there known firewall-related bugs or constraints (e.g., DNS inspection issues, NAT corner cases) that we must avoid during migrations?
rationale: Known platform bugs can be triggered by new patterns, causing outages mid-cutover.
evidence: TAC case logs, bug tracker notes, release notes.
red_flag: Yes, but only documented in personal notes or unknown details.

question: How is policy consistency maintained across multiple firewalls (central management in FMC/Firepower Management, templates, scripts)?
rationale: Inconsistent rules across sites lead to unpredictable behavior and security gaps.
evidence: FMC policies, automation repos, config snippets.
red_flag: Each firewall is configured manually and policy differs per site.

question: ⛔ For a cutover, what is the tested procedure to fail back to the previous firewall or policy set, and how long does that rollback take?
rationale: Lack of a fast rollback path makes any firewall change high-risk and hard to approve.
evidence: MoP rollback section, backup policies, copy start run, FMC deployment history.
red_flag: Rollback means manually undoing rules and reconfiguring interfaces with no timing estimate.

question: Which VPN technologies are in use today (site-to-site IPsec, DMVPN, FlexVPN, remote access, SSL VPN) and where are they terminated?
rationale: Knowing the mix and termination points is critical for migration and scaling.
evidence: show crypto ikev1 sa, show crypto ikev2 sa, show dmvpn, ASA/FTD VPN configs, design docs.
red_flag: We are not sure of all tunnels or some are only known to specific engineers.

question: For site-to-site tunnels, what topologies are used (hub-and-spoke, full mesh, partial mesh) and which hubs or route reflectors are critical?
rationale: Hub failure in hub-and-spoke can cause large outages; full mesh may not scale.
evidence: DMVPN/FlexVPN configs, BGP/OSPF over VPN design, topology diagrams.
red_flag: Critical sites rely on a single hub with no redundancy.

question: Which encryption and integrity algorithms and DH groups are currently used, and do they meet your security and performance requirements?
rationale: Weak or heavy algorithms can be non-compliant or overload hardware.
evidence: Crypto policies, show crypto ipsec sa detail, security standards.
red_flag: Outdated or weak crypto in production with compliance requirements.

question: How is keying handled (pre-shared keys vs certificates) and is there a centralized PKI for VPN certificates?
rationale: Scattered PSKs are hard to manage and rotate; certs need lifecycle planning.
evidence: Crypto maps/profiles, PKI docs, show crypto pki certificates, CA integration.
red_flag: Many shared PSKs used across tunnels with no inventory.

question: What is your long-term VPN framework preference (FlexVPN, DMVPN, SD-WAN, cloud VPN), and how will you converge disparate solutions?
rationale: Multiple frameworks without convergence plan create complexity and overhead.
evidence: Security roadmap, WAN strategy, vendor/tooling decisions.
red_flag: No long-term plan; new tunnels are built with whatever is easiest at the time.

question: For DMVPN/FlexVPN, how many spokes exist per hub and what are the current CPU, memory, and crypto throughput utilizations?
rationale: Overloaded hubs can cause intermittent tunnel outages and performance degradation.
evidence: show dmvpn, show crypto session, show process cpu, show platform hardware throughput.
red_flag: Hubs run consistently high CPU/throughput with continued spoke growth.

question: How is routing integrated over VPNs (static, BGP, EIGRP, OSPF), and do you limit routing updates to appropriate prefixes?
rationale: Poorly filtered VPN routing can leak routes and cause suboptimal paths.
evidence: Routing configs on VPN endpoints, route-maps, prefix-lists, show ip route.
red_flag: We redistribute everything into the VPN without controls.

question: How are remote access VPNs used (user populations, use-cases, peak concurrent sessions), and do you have capacity headroom for peak events?
rationale: Insufficient capacity can prevent remote work during incidents or surges.
evidence: ASA/FTD remote access stats, show vpn-sessiondb anyconnect, licensing.
red_flag: VPN regularly hits license/session limits or near 100% capacity.

question: What is the split tunneling policy for remote access and how do you control which traffic goes via VPN vs local Internet?
rationale: Overly permissive split tunneling may violate security policy, while no split may overload VPN/central links.
evidence: AnyConnect profiles, ASA group-policy config, security standards.
red_flag: We allow full split tunneling for all traffic without review.

question: How are remote VPN users authenticated and authorized (ISE, AD, LDAP, local) and which groups map to which VPN profiles/policies?
rationale: Unclear AAA mapping can give wrong access or lock users out.
evidence: ASA/FTD AAA config, ISE policy sets, AD group mapping.
red_flag: Single generic policy for all users or manual ACL updates.

question: How do you monitor VPN health (tunnel up/down, rekey failures, auth failures, throughput) and who responds to alerts?
rationale: Unmonitored VPNs can stay degraded for long periods.
evidence: NMS/SIEM dashboards, syslog, show crypto ikev2 sa, show vpn-sessiondb.
red_flag: VPN only checked when users complain; no proactive monitoring.

question: What is your rekey and lifetime strategy for IKE and IPsec SAs, and have you validated impact on CPU and session stability?
rationale: Poorly chosen lifetimes may cause CPU spikes or session drops during mass rekeys.
evidence: Crypto policy lifetimes, logs around rekey times, capacity reports.
red_flag: Default short lifetimes or no awareness of rekey behavior.

question: How will you migrate existing tunnels (per-branch/per-site) to any new headends or frameworks, and what is the fallback for each site?
rationale: VPN migrations can cut off entire sites if not carefully staged.
evidence: Migration design, per-site MoPs, tunnel lists with dependencies.
red_flag: We will reconfigure hubs and spokes in one go with no per-site rollback.

question: Will VPN endpoints’ public IPs or DNS names change, and if so, how will you propagate these changes to partners and clients?
rationale: Uncommunicated endpoint changes will break tunnels and client connectivity.
evidence: Public IP/DNS records, partner contacts, change notices.
red_flag: We expect partners to adjust quickly with minimal notice.

question: Do you have overlapping or private address spaces across VPNs, and how do you handle them (NAT, VRF, policy-based routing)?
rationale: Overlapping IPs can cause routing conflicts and misdelivery.
evidence: IP plan, VPN peer configs, NAT/VRF setups.
red_flag: Many overlapping ranges but no consistent solution.

question: How are VPN configuration changes governed (change tickets, maintenance windows), and how often do you review unused or legacy tunnels?
rationale: Accumulated legacy tunnels increase attack surface and complexity.
evidence: Change records, tunnel inventory, periodic review reports.
red_flag: No regular review; old tunnels remain indefinitely.

question: Are there any cloud-based VPN terminations (AWS/Azure/GCP gateways), and how are they integrated with on-prem routing and security?
rationale: Cloud VPNs require careful routing and security integration to avoid leaks.
evidence: Cloud networking configs, on-prem router/firewall configs, diagrams.
red_flag: Cloud VPNs set up ad-hoc without central design.

question: How do you handle user device security for remote access (posture checks, MFA, device certificates)?
rationale: Unsecured remote devices can be a major attack vector.
evidence: ISE/ASA/AnyConnect posture and MFA configs, security policies.
red_flag: Only username/password with no MFA or posture.

question: What is your incident response plan for VPN-related breaches or misconfigurations?
rationale: Clear playbooks reduce response time and damage during incidents.
evidence: IR runbooks, SOC procedures, past incident reports.
red_flag: No specific IR playbooks for VPN issues.

question: ⛔ If a new VPN design rollout causes widespread issues, what is the precise rollback strategy to the previous framework?
rationale: Rollback must be clear to avoid extended outages of remote sites/users.
evidence: MoP with rollback, old config backups, tested reversion procedure.
red_flag: Rollback is not fully documented or tested.

question: Which DNS platforms do you use (Windows, BIND, Infoblox, cloud), and which zones are authoritative internally vs externally?
rationale: Unclear authority leads to split-brain DNS or misdirected records during migration.
evidence: DNS architecture docs, zone listings, dig +trace, Infoblox/grid inventory.
red_flag: We are not sure which servers are authoritative for which zones.

question: Where are internal DNS servers physically and logically located (sites, subnets, VRFs), and how do clients reach them today?
rationale: DNS path changes during migration may break resolution or increase latency unexpectedly.
evidence: Network diagrams, IPAM, ip name-server configs, DHCP option 6/15, client settings.
red_flag: Some clients use random DNS servers hard-coded on endpoints.

question: What are the current TTL values for critical records (app VIPs, MX, public portals), and do you have a strategy to lower them before cutovers?
rationale: High TTLs cause slow propagation of changes, causing intermittent reachability issues.
evidence: Zone files, DNS management console, dig <record> +ttl.
red_flag: TTLs are long and we have no plan to adjust them before changes.

question: Are there any hard-coded IPs or hosts-file entries in servers, applications, or devices instead of using DNS?
rationale: Hard-coded IPs bypass DNS and will break on renumbering or VIP changes.
evidence: App documentation, OS hosts files, config management data.
red_flag: Many legacy apps have IPs hard-coded with no inventory.

question: How is DHCP delivered (Cisco IOS/IOS-XE, Windows, Infoblox, appliance), and where are the scopes defined for each site/VLAN?
rationale: Misaligned DHCP scopes cause addressing conflicts or clients getting addresses from the wrong scope.
evidence: DHCP server config, show running-config | section dhcp, Infoblox/Windows DHCP console.
red_flag: We are not sure which scopes serve which VLANs or overlapping scopes.

question: Which interfaces and VLANs have IP helper addresses configured, and where do they point today?
rationale: Incorrect or missing helpers break DHCP for entire user segments, especially during migration.
evidence: show run | include ip helper-address, interface configs, DHCP design doc.
red_flag: We configure helpers ad-hoc or Some VLANs rely on local, undocumented DHCP servers.

question: What are the current DHCP lease times per scope (especially for user/voice vs servers), and will you shorten them ahead of addressing changes?
rationale: Long leases cause slow convergence to new addressing and overlapping usage during migration.
evidence: DHCP scope settings, show ip dhcp pool, server DHCP console.
red_flag: All scopes use long default leases (e.g., 8 days) with no plan to reduce before change.

question: Do you use DHCP reservations for infrastructure (printers, APs, IP phones), and are they documented and easy to migrate?
rationale: Unaccounted reservations may be lost or misapplied during scope migration.
evidence: DHCP reservation lists, CMDB, export files from DHCP servers.
red_flag: Reservations exist but only on legacy servers with no central documentation.

question: Is there a central IPAM system (Infoblox, NetBox, custom) that is authoritative for IP space, VLANs, and DNS/DHCP integration?
rationale: Without a single IPAM, IP conflicts and inconsistent records are likely during renumbering.
evidence: IPAM database, integration docs, DHCP/DNS synchronization configuration.
red_flag: We track IPs in spreadsheets or multiple unsynced IP lists.

question: How are forward and reverse DNS zones managed, and do you maintain accurate PTR records for servers and infrastructure IPs?
rationale: Missing PTRs degrade troubleshooting and some security tools; inconsistent reverse zones suggest poor hygiene.
evidence: DNS zone configuration, dig -x <ip>, DNS/IPAM integration reports.
red_flag: We rarely maintain PTR records or many stale reverse-zone entries.

question: Are there split-horizon DNS views (internal vs external answers) and how are these implemented and documented?
rationale: Misconfigured views can cause users to see wrong IPs depending on location, especially during migration.
evidence: DNS view configurations, design docs, dig from internal/external vantage points.
red_flag: Some zones behave differently but not fully documented.

question: How is DHCP failover or redundancy implemented (split scope, active/standby, load sharing) and when was it last tested?
rationale: Unverified DHCP redundancy leads to widespread outages on a single-server failure.
evidence: DHCP failover configs, test reports, logs during failover tests.
red_flag: Single DHCP server per site or Failover has never been tested.

question: ⛔ During migration, what is the exact order of operations for changing DNS records, DHCP helpers, and routes, and how will you validate each step?
rationale: Out-of-order changes can cause black holes, misdirected traffic, and long troubleshooting during cutover.
evidence: MoP, sequencing diagrams, dig, ipconfig /renew, show ip route, show ip dhcp binding.
red_flag: We will update DNS/DHCP during the window without a defined sequence.

question: For any public-facing records (web, VPN, APIs), what is the rollback plan if a DNS change causes service impact?
rationale: Lack of rollback for DNS changes can prolong outages due to caching.
evidence: DNS change procedures, registrar interface access, dig tests, monitoring dashboards.
red_flag: Rollback means manually editing records with no pre-defined plan or lowered TTLs.

question: Are there DHCP options that bake in infrastructure IPs (e.g., option 150 for CUCM, option 43 for APs) that must be updated during renumbering?
rationale: Forgotten options break phones, APs, and specialized devices even when addressing looks correct.
evidence: DHCP option configuration, CUCM/voice design docs, WLAN controller docs.
red_flag: We are not sure which options are in use per scope.

question: How are DNS and DHCP logs stored and analyzed, and do you have visibility into misconfigured clients or conflicts?
rationale: Lack of log analysis hides systemic misconfigurations and address conflicts.
evidence: Syslog/SIEM integrations, DHCP conflict logs, DNS query logs.
red_flag: Logs exist but nobody reviews them or short retention only.

question: Are there external dependencies on your DNS zones (third-party integrations, partners, SaaS callbacks) that need coordination for changes?
rationale: External consumers can break if their whitelists or configs are not updated in sync.
evidence: Integration docs, partner agreements, app owner interviews.
red_flag: We do not know who depends on our DNS records externally.

question: Do any security controls depend on DNS (DNS firewall, RPZ, threat feeds, DNS-based load balancing), and how will these behave during migration?
rationale: DNS security features can silently block or redirect traffic if not updated with new IPs or zones.
evidence: DNS firewall/RPZ configs, security docs, load balancer/DNS GSLB configs.
red_flag: We turned on some DNS security but it is poorly documented.

question: After DHCP/DNS/IPAM changes, what specific validation tests will you run (per VLAN, per site, per critical app), and who owns them?
rationale: Without explicit tests, DNS/DHCP issues may surface only after users are impacted.
evidence: MoP test plan, UAT scripts, nslookup/dig, client renew/lease checks.
red_flag: We rely on users to report resolution or lease issues or no structured testing.

question: ⛔ When decommissioning old DNS/DHCP/IPAM servers, how will you ensure there are no remaining clients or records depending on them?
rationale: Premature decommissioning can cause subtle, hard-to-trace outages.
evidence: Traffic captures, logs showing queries/requests, gradual disablement plan, monitoring for lingering use.
red_flag: We will just shut down the old servers after the change window with no monitoring period.

question: Which load balancer platforms are in use (F5, Citrix/NetScaler, Cisco ACE/CSM, cloud LBs), and where are they placed in the traffic path (one-arm vs inline)?
rationale: Platform and topology drive how VIPs, routing, and security policies interact during migration.
evidence: Network diagrams, LB inventory, tmsh list ltm virtual (F5), NetScaler config export.
red_flag: We are not entirely sure or mixed topologies with no documentation.

question: For each LB, what is the software version and HA model (active/standby, active/active, device group/cluster), and when was failover last tested?
rationale: Unverified HA or outdated code makes LB a single point of failure during cutovers.
evidence: tmsh show sys version, tmsh show cm failover-status (F5), HA test reports, vendor lifecycle docs.
red_flag: Failover was never tested or We rarely patch load balancers.

question: Is there a complete VIP inventory (VIP IP, DNS name, ports, associated pool, business owner, criticality), and is it kept up to date?
rationale: Missing VIP inventory makes it impossible to plan or validate migrations safely.
evidence: LB config export, CMDB/service catalog, F5 tmsh list ltm virtual.
red_flag: We do not have a single, accurate VIP list or unknown owners.

question: How is server health monitored (L3/L4 vs L7 monitors, custom URIs, intervals/timeouts) and what happens when a health check fails?
rationale: Weak monitors either send traffic to broken servers or mark healthy servers down, both problematic.
evidence: F5 monitor definitions, tmsh list ltm monitor, NetScaler/ADC monitor config, health check docs.
red_flag: Only basic TCP checks for complex apps or unknown behavior on failure.

question: What persistence methods are used per VIP (source IP, cookie, SSL ID, RADIUS AVP), and what are the timeout values?
rationale: Wrong persistence breaks stateful or multi-step transactions; too-long timeouts can overload specific nodes.
evidence: LB profiles, tmsh list ltm persistence, ADC policy view, app design docs.
red_flag: We use default or random persistence or We do not know.

question: Which VIPs perform SSL termination/offload vs SSL passthrough, and where are the certificates and keys stored and managed?
rationale: Certificate management and crypto posture affect compliance and migration complexity.
evidence: SSL profile configs, cert/key stores on LB, PKI inventory, tmsh list ltm profile client-ssl.
red_flag: Certificates are manual and not tracked or Same key on many devices without control.

question: How do you handle X-Forwarded-For / client IP preservation, and do any backend apps rely on client IP or other LB-injected headers?
rationale: Apps depending on client IP may break when LB topology or SNAT behavior changes.
evidence: HTTP profiles, app server configs, developer documentation.
red_flag: Apps rely on client IP but we use SNAT without headers or unknown behavior.

question: What is the routing model for one-arm VIPs (SNAT, policy-based routing, WCCP) and how is asymmetric routing avoided?
rationale: Asymmetric paths with firewalls or stateful devices can cause session drops.
evidence: LB SNAT/PBR configs, firewall routing, tmsh list ltm virtual and SNAT pools, routing diagrams.
red_flag: We rely on default routing with stateful devices in path.

question: For GSLB or multi-site VIPs, how are health, proximity, and stickiness decisions made (DNS-based, anycast, BGP), and who owns those policies?
rationale: Poor GSLB can send users to unhealthy or distant sites and complicate DR.
evidence: GSLB configs (F5 DNS, NetScaler GSLB), DNS zone configs, routing policies.
red_flag: GSLB was set up by a vendor years ago; nobody touches it.

question: Are there any shared VIPs or multi-tenant LBs where different apps share the same IP/ports, and how is change impact assessed?
rationale: Shared VIPs create blast radius where one change impacts multiple apps.
evidence: LB config, app inventory, change logs.
red_flag: Many apps share generic VIPs with no segregation or owner mapping.

question: How are LB configurations version-controlled and backed up, and how would you restore a single VIP or the whole device after a failed change?
rationale: Lack of backups and versioning makes rollback from logical misconfigurations slow and risky.
evidence: Config backup tool, git/automation repos, vendor backup commands (F5 UCS/archive).
red_flag: We take manual backups occasionally or no ability to restore granular configs.

question: ⛔ During network or DC migrations, will VIP IPs change, and what is the strategy for DNS updates, TTL adjustments, and parallel operation?
rationale: VIP IP changes without coordinated DNS and cutover plan cause intermittent or prolonged outages.
evidence: Migration plan, DNS records, dig, LB migration runbooks, app owner approvals.
red_flag: We will update DNS in the window and hope caches expire quickly.

question: For internal APIs and microservices, are they fronted by LBs, service meshes, or both, and how does that affect routing and security policies?
rationale: Overlapping layers of load balancing and policy can create confusing traffic flows.
evidence: Kubernetes/mesh configs, LB configs, app architecture docs.
red_flag: We have both but no clear design on which traffic uses what.

question: What rate-limiting, WAF, or DDoS protections are active on the LBs, and do they have app-specific tuning?
rationale: Untuned protections can block legitimate traffic or fail to protect critical services.
evidence: WAF policy configs, rate-limit profiles, security reports.
red_flag: We run default WAF/rate limits with frequent false positives or disabled features.

question: How are health monitors tuned for ISE/RADIUS or other auth services behind LBs (especially persistence keyed on Calling-Station-ID for ISE)?
rationale: Incorrect monitors or persistence can break 802.1X and NAC during load balancer or PSN failures.
evidence: LB RADIUS health monitor configs, persistence profiles, ISE load-balancing guide.
red_flag: We only check UDP 1812 is open or short persistence timers for RADIUS.

question: What metrics and dashboards exist for LB performance (connections, CPU, memory, per-VIP stats), and who monitors them?
rationale: Overloaded LBs or misbehaving VIPs may not be noticed until outages occur.
evidence: NMS integration, LB stats exports, F5 tmsh show ltm virtual, NetScaler observability.
red_flag: We rarely look at LB performance or no integration with monitoring.

question: Are there any application migrations already planned that will change backends (e.g., to Kubernetes or cloud) during the network migration program?
rationale: Simultaneous app and network changes complicate attribution and rollback.
evidence: App roadmap, project portfolio, DevOps discussions.
red_flag: Multiple major app moves coincide with this network migration, without coordination.

question: How do you handle blue/green or canary deployments with LBs (weights, separate VIPs, path-based routing), and is that process standardized?
rationale: Non-standard rollout methods increase risk of misrouting or overloading new versions.
evidence: LB policies, deployment runbooks, CI/CD integration docs.
red_flag: Each team does their own thing with no shared pattern.

question: For each critical VIP, who is the business owner and what are their SLOs (availability, latency), and is there an agreed test plan for cutovers?
